turn_text: One of the things that I guess was rumored a few days ago, because you've had the controversy of the debt ceiling, and then you've got the democratic voter rights initiatives, they were sort of this threat that they would pull the plug on the filibuster. From your view, I guess, let me do a question, sort of, in this day and age, what role and what's the importance of the filibuster, and then two, Do you think it is seriously threatened at this time?

Well, I think that Leader McConnell thought it was threatened last week. His view, which I'm not sure I share, but there's no way to know if it was right or not, is that this maybe was the one moment where our two stalwarts on the other side, mansion and cinema, would decide, OK, if the Republicans aren't going to help us to see that the government pays its bills, maybe we're going to have to change the rules for this one thing. And you can't change the rules for one thing. Two reasons for it. One is probably just you can't reverse the parliamentarian and do that in a targeted way. And even if you could, If you ever change the cloture rule in the Senate, and I'll talk more about that in a second. If you ever change the cloture rule in the Senate for, say, paying the bills the government owes money to, why would you then not change it to protect our democracy? Or why would you not change it to do whatever is the next thing to save the planet? It was more important to pay people money that the government owed money to than it is to save the planet. It won't work that way. We used to have a room when I was the whip in the house. And only two people, you mentioned this, only two people in the history of the country have been elected leaders in both the House and Senate. And I'm one of them, so it must not be a very smart thing to have been willing to do. When I was in the whip in the house, we had in the house there was a rule called the motion to recommit. And on every bill, you have a chance that goes through the regular process to send it back to committee to do X. And X usually sounded pretty good. Send it back to committee to add this to it. And you know, my rule is the whip and generally the rule in the house had been, if you never vote for one of these, it's fine because you say, no, that was just a procedural thing to kill the bill. But if you ever voted for one of them, what about the next thing that comes along? Is it less important than, you know, you vote for Second Amendment issue one day, and the next day the motion recommit is about the value of motherhood. And so you're for the Second Amendment, but you're not for the value of motherhood, you can't go down that line. You can't, you can't, you can, I don't think you can ever selectively eliminate the super majority in the Senate that shouldn't be overused, but it's there. And why does it define the Senate? The cloture rule, where it takes 60 votes to begin a debate, and 60 votes to end a debate, the cloture rule really requires you to find friends on the other side. The Democrats, two or three times in the history of the country, have had more than two thirds of the Senate. Republicans have never had more than 56 popularly elected Republican senators. That's our all time high. And the Democrats haven't had many more than that very many times. So what that rule does is it makes you seek out people on the other side that you don't agree with on everything, but you do agree with on at least one thing. And so, you know, I could go down to Senator Stabino and I, Debbie Stabino from Michigan have done a lot of work on mental health. treating mental health like all other health. Chris Coons and I every year reauthorized the Victims of Child Abuse Act, even though oddly the Obama administration tried to eliminate it two times. But we do that. Sherrod Brown, who I've known for 35 years, and we've agreed on exactly five things in 35 years, and they're all federal law. And everything from a bill we did on advanced manufacturing to all women who have breast cancer surgery have to be told all their options. And we have to have a pretty strong, wide expanse to find that five things we agree with. But it makes you better friends. We've been friends for 35 years. But once you pass that first bill together, you think, well, let's find something else we can do together. And there's a much longer list of those members than I just went through. And I think it does define the Senate. It also means if you have to have a super majority in the Senate, The country really has to feel pretty strongly about something for quite a while. You know, if you look at the house, often these things don't become law because of the Senate, but there'll be an election and the House majority changes and three or four major bills passed that would hedge you in a really different direction and they die in the Senate because the Senate wasn't impacted by the very last election like the House was. And by the time you get through two or three Senate cycles, countries usually change its mind. And so, you know, we're not radically going this way and then radically coming back the other way. And I think the cloture rule, the filibuster rule in the Senate has developed, not sure it's exactly what the founders thought would happen, but it developed in a way that it almost requires the country to think a little bit about what it believes it wants to do.
